scenes.narration: Heian-kyo, the capital of Japan, was founded in 794, and it was laid out with the sky in mind. Its planners believed that mountains, rivers and compass directions carried invisible power. The court that lived there ran on omens. A comet, a fire, a strange dream, even a crow at the wrong gate could change the calendar of state. To read such signs, the government employed specialists. They were not wandering mystics. They were salaried officials, and their office was called the Onmyoryo, the Bureau of Yin and Yang.

scenes.narration: The Bureau sat inside the imperial administration, and it practiced three main crafts: astronomy, the calendar, and divination. Astronomers watched the heavens and reported anything unusual. Calendar masters calculated the days and the months. Diviners judged which days were lucky for a journey, a wedding or a ceremony, and which ones to avoid. Courtiers consulted them the way a modern ministry might be consulted. Their work was careful and technical. And into this world, according to tradition in the year 921, a boy named Abe no Seimei was born.

scenes.narration: Almost nothing is known about his childhood. The Abe family was not among the great houses of the capital, and no one wrote down the early years of a boy with modest prospects. What is clear is that Seimei became a student of the Kamo family, the leading masters of the Bureau's crafts. Tradition names Kamo no Tadayuki as his first teacher, and Tadayuki's son Yasunori as the master who shaped him. Seimei did not storm the court. He began like every other official: as an apprentice, learning one patient observation at a time.

scenes.narration: Astronomy was the most delicate of the Bureau's crafts. Each night, a duty astronomer watched the stars from a platform, noting the movement of planets, the appearance of comets and the path of the moon. Any reading had to be exact. A comet or an eclipse was not scenery; it was a message addressed to the emperor, and misreading it could shake a reign. For Seimei, the work was slow, cold and solitary, and it was the foundation of everything that followed. He was learning that in the court, whoever interprets the sky holds a quiet power.

scenes.narration: The earliest trace of Seimei in the records dates to 960, when he was already nearly forty and still only an advanced student of astronomy. That is late for a rising star, and it tells us something important: he was not a prodigy. He was a patient professional. By 972 he had become the court's Doctor of Astronomy. And when his master Yasunori died in 977, tradition says the Kamo family's calendar craft passed to Yasunori's own son, while Seimei inherited the astronomy. The heavens, in effect, were now his to read.

scenes.narration: By the 980s, the sky was no longer only a matter of study. The court was a place of intense rivalry, and the most powerful family was the Fujiwara, who ruled by marrying their daughters to emperors. In 986, the young Emperor Kazan suddenly left the palace at night and took Buddhist vows, tricked by the Fujiwara schemers who wanted a child of their own blood on the throne. That child, a boy of just six, became Emperor Ichijo. And it is on this very night that one of the most famous Seimei legends is set.

scenes.narration: The legend, written down about a century after Seimei's death, goes like this. As Kazan slipped away, his path took him past Seimei's house. Inside, Seimei saw a sign in the heavens and cried out that the emperor was abdicating. He ordered one of his shikigami, the spirit servants of his craft, to go to the palace. An unseen hand pushed the door open, and a voice answered that the emperor was passing by at that very moment. It is a wonderful story, but no source from Seimei's own time records it. We should treat it as folklore.

scenes.narration: What the sources do show is a court that was becoming dependent on him. By the 990s, Fujiwara no Michinaga was moving to the center of power. In 995, a wave of illness killed several senior Fujiwara, and Michinaga, a younger son, rose unexpectedly to lead the court. Michinaga was a man who tracked taboos, lucky days and omens with great care. In his own diary and in other courtiers' journals, we see officials of the Bureau, Seimei among them, called upon to advise on ceremonies and safe dates.

scenes.narration: Seimei's value was not magic. It was certainty. When a decision had to be made, Michinaga could ask whether a day was safe, whether a direction was forbidden, whether a strange event meant danger. The answer came from a trained official with an old, respected method. It gave Michinaga cover to act, delay or refuse. In a court where every move might be read as an insult, an authoritative no, or an authoritative yes, was worth more than any army. And Seimei, now in his seventies, was the voice that could give it.

scenes.narration: Picture what an omen meant at that level. An astronomer on the platform spots something wrong in the sky and reports it, and within hours the whole palace reacts. The emperor might withdraw into ritual seclusion, ceremonies might be postponed, and special rites might be ordered across the capital. Everyone waited for the Bureau to explain what the heavens wanted. In these moments, the old, quiet man with the white beard held an influence far beyond his modest rank. He did not command armies. He told the court how to be afraid, and what to do about it.

scenes.narration: The most famous legend of all comes from a collection of tales written about two centuries later. It says Michinaga was entering a temple he had founded when his white dog refused to let him pass through the gate. Seimei was summoned, and declared that someone had buried a curse beneath the path. Two clay dishes, bound together, were dug up, and the plot was undone. The tale names a rival sorcerer as the culprit. But that temple was built years after Seimei's death. The story is invented, yet it shows how deeply the court remembered his reputation.

scenes.narration: In the end, Seimei died at an advanced age in 1005, in his mid-eighties, an astonishing age for the eleventh century. He had served through the reigns of five emperors and lived to see Michinaga stand at the summit of the court. No miracle marks his death in the records we trust. He had simply outlived nearly everyone who knew the court when he first entered it, and he left behind a craft, a family and a name.

scenes.narration: Two years after his death, in 1007, Emperor Ichijo is said to have ordered a shrine built on the site of Seimei's home in Kyoto. That is the shrine's own tradition, and Seimei Shrine still stands there today. His descendants carried his name forward. Over the centuries his line became the Tsuchimikado family, which led the court's masters of yin and yang and, in time, dominated Japan's official divination right into the nineteenth century. A career that began with a patient apprentice had become an inheritance.

scenes.narration: As the centuries passed, the official became a wizard. Tale collections described him killing a frog with nothing but a blade of grass, and keeping spirit servants who opened and closed his doors. Later storytellers and playwrights gave him a mother who was a fox, named Kuzunoha, and a bitter rivalry with a sorcerer named Ashiya Doman. These stories grew far beyond anything the court diaries say. They were told in theaters and on storytellers' lips, and each retelling made Seimei more magical, and less like the man who actually lived.

scenes.narration: The institution that Seimei served outlived him by more than eight centuries. Generation after generation, the Bureau of Yin and Yang kept watching the sky and drawing up the calendar for the court. Then, in the nineteenth century, Japan opened itself to Western science. The new Meiji government abolished the Bureau in 1870 and adopted the Western calendar not long after. The craft Seimei had mastered was officially over, but his name had already escaped the archives and entered the imagination of an entire culture.

scenes.narration: So why did the court trust a man with a divining board and a brush? Because a society that fears uncertainty will pay anyone who seems to reduce it. Seimei offered a method, a lineage and a calm voice. His advice told emperors when to move and when to wait, and it gave the powerful a language to justify their choices. Whether the heavens truly spoke was almost beside the point. What mattered was that everyone believed that someone could hear them.

scenes.narration: That is the most reliable picture historians can draw. Seimei was a gifted official, serious about method and valued by the most powerful people in Japan. His influence came not from spells, but from information and trust. He told the court what the sky showed and what the calendar allowed. The rest, the demons, the curses, the fox mother, was added later by people who needed his story to be larger than life. Legends grow around a person precisely when the real person has left too little behind to contradict them.

scenes.narration: Today, Abe no Seimei is one of the most famous figures of the Heian period, in Japan and far beyond. Novels, films and manga have turned him into a hero who battles spirits with paper charms, and his five-pointed star crest is recognized across the country. Pilgrims still visit his shrine in Kyoto and leave offerings. This is the paradox of his life. The truth, a careful, loyal official reading the stars, is quieter than any story. And yet the story is the reason we remember him.
